title: Stanley Dance's South America story and talk of Jim Crow laws
summary: Stanley recalls being refused boarding in Brazil with Ellington's band because he was white; McShann and Stanley agree such laws were a hangover from slavery.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I was in South America with Duke and they were loading the plane up, half of it with melons and half with people. So the band -- he had a white bass player. His instrument had gone through with all the others. So now they've got to load Duke Ellington's band on. They all went on the plane. They wouldn't let the bass player and me through because we were white and they thought, "You don't belong with them." We had a big argument before we could get on the plane.
They wouldn't let Ellington's band through?
They let Duke through. They wouldn't let (inaudible).

They let Duke -- they knew the band, you see, so there was the bass player and I. We come up to go and they wouldn't let us through and we couldn't talk any Portuguese. Eventually Paul Gonsalves came up and explained the whole thing.

Well, you know, you find all these different laws and things and I think why you ran into so much of that, people were making laws for their own conveniences during those times, you know, and the people thought -- didn't think big -- the people, I think, and it shows the way they thought small, you know what I mean?
That was a hangover from slavery.
I mean, it was a matter of keeping the people down. That's really what it was, wasn't it?
You know, and they'd do it as long as they could get away with it.
